title: Hipparcos (1989-1993) and TESS (2018-2026) eclipse depths agree within 5 percent for most of 1,086 bright eclipsing binaries; V2133 Cyg and V444 Cep had about 1.5 times deeper eclipses in 1991
abstract: Question: do the eclipse depths of bright eclipsing binaries change over 30 years? Approach: for 1,086 binaries with Hipparcos epoch photometry (1989-1993) and TESS 2-minute light curves (2018-2026), we fitted the TESS phase template to the Hipparcos epochs with a free depth scale and time shift. A second, template-free test searched for eclipses that Hipparcos saw but TESS does not show. Result: in a clean sample of 327 binaries the Hipparcos/TESS depth ratio has a median of 1.036 and a robust scatter of 0.053 in ln(ratio). 23 binaries differ by more than 3 sigma (0.9 expected). Most of these have known causes (crowding, saturation, spots, peculiar stars, period changes, band effects). After vetting with all TESS sectors, a day-block bootstrap and a blackbody band envelope, two binaries had clearly deeper eclipses in 1991: V2133 Cyg (1.59 times, 95 percent range 1.34-1.74; nine stable TESS sectors; the secondary eclipse was 3 times deeper, opposite to a band effect) and V444 Cep (1.46 times, range 1.33-1.61; grazing eclipses of near-equal stars, band limit 1.03). V542 Lyr, AE Pic and HIP 65380 are probable cases. The template-free test recovers the known vanished system HS Hya (0.20 mag in 1991, below 0.0075 in TESS) and finds no other lost eclipses. Thus about 1.5 percent of bright binaries (5 of 327) changed depth by more than 35 percent in 30 years, which needs orbital-plane changes of about 1 degree. Limitations: one Hipparcos epoch with about 100 points per star, a scaled template instead of a physical model, a blackbody band model, TESS saturation for three of the five candidates, and no spectroscopy to identify third bodies.
